title: Using Virtual Reality to Evaluate the Impact of Room Acoustics on Cognitive Performance and Well-Being
research_question: To test whether an acoustic intervention focused on reducing reverberation can be simulated successfully in VR, and to ascertain its effects on cognitive performance and well-being.

participants.description: 42 participants (35 female, 7 male) aged 18-29 years (M=20.69, SD=2.44). 81% were undergraduate university students. Participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and normal hearing. 39 data sets for physiological measures.
participants.recruitment: Facebook, email, and the university's psychology student participation pool

stimuli_or_exposures.description: A virtual open-plan classroom environment (18x14m plan, 2.8m ceiling height, 560m³ volume) developed in Unity game engine. Visuals included plasterboard walls with absorbent panels and thin carpet. Acoustic rendering prepared in ODEON Auditorium Room Acoustic Software Version 14, generating 3D impulse responses. MAX MSP Version 8 used to convolve anechoic/quasi-anechoic speech and noise with impulse responses to create ambisonic audio. Presented via HTC VIVO-Pro Eye VR Headset and calibrated Beyerdynamic DT 860 open-back stereo headphones. Three acoustic conditions were simulated: No Ambient Noise (control), Untreated with Noise (typical open-plan classroom ambient noise without acoustic treatment, T30=0.9s, C50=4dB), and Treated with Noise (same ambient noise with acoustic treatment to reduce reverberation via absorbent ceiling tiles, T30=0.5s, C50=13dB). All conditions presented at 52-56 dB LAeq.
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Methods, Acoustic Conditions, Figure 1, Table 1, Table 2

measures.instrument: Auditory n-back task (0-back for low cognitive load, 2-back for high cognitive load)
Auditory n-back task (0-back for low cognitive load, 2-back for high cognitive load)

findings.antecedent: Acoustic condition (No Ambient Noise, Untreated with Noise, Treated with Noise)
findings.mechanism: Ambient noise makes it cognitively more challenging to attend to, increasing task response time; acoustic treatment reduces reverberation, decreasing perceptual and cognitive demands.
findings.quote: The results revealed a significant main effect of acoustics, F (2,82) = 5.38, p = 0.006, η2 partial = 0.12.
A statistically significant main effect of cognitive load (i.e. 2-back vs. 0-back) was also found, F (1,41) = 44.57, p > 0.001, η2 partial = 0.52.
A nonsignificant interaction of Acoustics × Cognitive Load was revealed, F (2,82) = 1.15, p = 0.321.

findings.mechanism: Irrelevant ambient noise increases cognitive demands, leading to slower response times.
findings.quote: the no background sound condition led to significantly faster response times (M = 788.97, SE = 14.58) than the untreated sound condition (M = 817.73, SE = 16.28; p = 0.042).

findings.mechanism: Acoustical treatment successfully reduced the negative impact of background sound on cognitive performance by reducing reverberation.
findings.quote: Further, the untreated sound condition presented significantly slower response times (M = 817.73, SE = 16.28) than the treated sound condition (M = 789.55, SE = 15.76; p = 0.012).

findings.antecedent: No Ambient Noise acoustic condition vs. Treated with Noise acoustic condition
findings.mechanism: The acoustic treatment effectively mitigated the negative impact of ambient noise, making performance indistinguishable from a no-noise environment.
findings.quote: There was no significant difference between the no background sound condition (M = 788.97, SE = 14.58) and the treated sound condition (M = 789.55, SE = 15.76; p = 1.00) response times.

findings.mechanism: Noise was not disruptive enough or task duration too short to cause robust physiological changes.
findings.quote: No significant main effect of acoustics was found, F (2,76) = 0.17, p = 0.840.
Further, no significant interactive effect of Acoustics × Cognitive Load was revealed, F (1.68, 63.96 Greenhouse-Geisser) = 0.34, p = 0.677.

findings.mechanism: Higher cognitive load increases physiological arousal.
findings.quote: The results revealed, however, a significant main effect of cognitive load, F (1,38) = 5.03, p =0.031, η2 partial=0.12.

findings.mechanism: Noise was not disruptive enough or task duration too short to cause robust physiological changes.
findings.quote: The results revealed a nonsignificant effect of acoustic condition F (2,76) = 0.42, p = 0.660
and a further nonsignificant Acoustics × Cognitive Load interaction F (2, 76) = 0.77, p = 0.467.

findings.mechanism: Higher cognitive load increases physiological arousal.
findings.quote: The results revealed, however, a significant effect of cognitive load on heart rate, F (1,38) = 16.50, p < 0.001, η2 partial = 30.

findings.mechanism: Noise was not disruptive enough or task duration too short to cause robust physiological changes.
findings.quote: There was no statistically significant main effect of acoustics on heart rate variability, F (2,76) = 1.33, p = 0.270.
The results further revealed the Acoustics × Cognitive Load interaction was nonsignificant, F (2,76 Greenhouse-Geisser) = 3.30, p = 0.050, η2 partial = 0.08.

findings.mechanism: Higher cognitive load decreases vagal tone, indicating increased physiological stress.
findings.quote: The results revealed, however, a significant main effect of cognitive load, F (1,38) = 24.45, p < 0.001, η2 partial = 0.39.

findings.mechanism: Noise was not disruptive enough or task duration too short to cause robust affective changes.
findings.quote: The one-way repeated measures MANOVA revealed that overall the factors of acoustics had a nonsignificant effect on mood, F (4,164) = 2.20, p = 0.071.

mechanisms: Irrelevant ambient noise (background chatter) increases cognitive demands and makes it more challenging to attend to, leading to slower response times.
Acoustic interventions that reduce reverberation decrease perceptual and cognitive demands, thereby mitigating the negative effects of noise on cognitive performance.
Higher cognitive load increases physiological arousal (skin conductance, heart rate) and decreases heart rate variability.
implementation_implications: VR provides an effective and efficient means to evaluate the cognitive effects of acoustic interventions before physical installation.
High-fidelity-dynamic VR simulations of the built environment can help create optimal conditions for performance and well-being.

tables.description: Sound absorption coefficients of key materials used in the virtual classroom model across octave band centre frequencies.
Octave Band Leq Sound Pressure Levels at the participant location for n-back speech and ambient noise in treated and untreated scenarios.

Means and Standard Deviations of response accuracy, response time, skin conductance, heart rate, and heart rate variability for 0-Back and 2-Back conditions across No Ambient Noise, Noise (without treatment), and Noise (with treatment) acoustic conditions.

limitations: The ambient noise might not have been disruptive enough (low intelligibility of background chatter) or the task duration (3 min per condition) too short to cause robust physiological and affective changes.
The participant sample consisted primarily of academically high-performing female university students, who may be less susceptible to noise effects.
The study did not compare VR with a real-life classroom, so it could not determine if the effects of noise are identical to real-world settings.
Current acoustic modeling algorithms may generate plausible but not entirely authentic simulations, distinguishable from recordings by human observers.
The control condition of no background noise is likely impossible to achieve in real-world shared work and study settings.

paper_metadata.title: Using Virtual Reality to Evaluate the Impact of Room Acoustics on Cognitive Performance and Well-Being
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Using Virtual Reality to Evaluate the Impact of Room Acoustics on Cognitive Performance and Well-Being
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Irrelevant ambient noise can have profound effects on human performance and wellbeing. Acoustic interventions (e.g., installation of sound absorbing materials) that reduce intelligible noise (i.e., sound unrelated to the relevant speech, including noise from other talkers within the space) by reducing room reverberation, have been found to be an effective means to alleviate the negative effects of noise on cognitive performance. However, these interventions are expensive, and it is difficult to evaluate their impact in the field. Virtual reality (VR) provides a promising simulation platform to evaluate the likely impact of varied acoustic interventions before they are chosen and installed. This study employed a virtual classroom environment to evaluate whether an intervention to reduce reverberation can be simulated successfully in VR and mitigate the effects of ambient noise on cognitive performance, physiological stress, and mood. The repeated-measures experimental design consisted of three acoustic conditions: no ambient noise, typical open-plan classroom ambient noise without acoustic treatment, and the same ambient noise with acoustic treatment to reduce reverberation. Results revealed that ambient noise negatively affected participants’ cognitive performance but had no measurable effect on physiological stress or self-reported mood. Importantly, the negative effect of ambient noise was completely ameliorated by the acoustic treatment (i.e. indistinguishable from performance in the no noise condition). The study shows that VR provides an effective and efficient means to evaluate the cognitive effects of acoustic interventions.
